So that's what I hope to cover this evening. So on the first slide, just wanted to acknowledge that conservation authorities and municipalities very much have a shared goal, and that is sustainable economic development. We recognize it's a big focus of not only our member municipalities, but the province, to always be increasing economic development opportunities, primarily housing as well right now is huge topic of interest and a real need to increase the housing supply. And when you look at, as a municipality or the province, wanting new development, redevelopment, and ultimately recreation and tourism as well, it's all to also grow your tax base. And when we look at that as the goal, there's a few things you need to do to accomplish that. And one is you need to make sure you have the ingredients in place to enable development, and that would include having potable water supply. So you can only increase housing, increase growth, if you have enough drinking water and drinking water of a quality that's potable for new communities and expanding communities. You obviously need land supply to be able to facilitate increased development. And then also green space is attractive for recreation and tourism and clean lakes and rivers. We've seen it time and time again that when you have algae blooms or decreased water quality, you start to see property values decrease and also decrease in interest from tourists and also recreational opportunities. So how do we accomplish those goals? Well, it's really about avoiding natural hazards. So the one that most people are familiar with is areas that are prone to flooding. So trying to direct development away from floodplains, and that's not only to protect obviously people and their primary investment, which is their home, but anytime you increase development in a floodplain, you're really dispersing those floodwaters to another property. And so you can actually inadvertently impact your land supply by forcing floodwater onto other property that wouldn't normally flood. Also important to protect natural features. So we know that areas that are wooded and also wetlands, they act like sponges. So they slow down runoff and they hold water. And this helps actually reduce the overall impact of flooding. So without those types of natural features, we would actually have larger floodplains which would further decrease your land supply. Managing runoff is for the same reason, but also to ensure that we're protecting water quality. So anytime we have nutrients or contaminants running off into lakes and rivers, that's typically where you run into water quality problems or issues with algae blooms. Runoff can also impact your drinking water, whether you're drawing from groundwater or surface water. And last is protecting sources of drinking water. So in the Montague context, most of your development would be on private servicing. So wanting to make sure that any redevelopment or especially new development is taking place in areas where we won't impact the quality or the quantity of groundwater. And obviously across our watershed, we have a lot of thin soils, a lot of rock, bedrock at surface, and it can be fractured in some areas. And this poses a real challenge for private development in the sense that septic systems can be a source of contamination and can actually impact the aquifers that private wells are drawing from. So that's a constraint and a challenge for development in our area. So how do we accomplish the sustainable economic development? It's really a couple of different phases. So municipalities and conservation authorities work closely at two key stages. One is land use planning. So anytime somebody has a development project, we always encourage them to go to the municipality first to understand what approvals they may need under land use planning. So at the county level in Lanark, the county's responsible for official plan amendments, subdivision approvals, and severances. And then at the lower tier level, you take care of zoning bylaw amendments, site plan control, minor variants. So it's really important before somebody begin a development to understand if they will need any one of those planning approvals. And when they make an application to either the lower tier or upper tier municipality, that application is circulated to conservation authorities. And we comment on a few key areas, including natural hazards. So that would be flood plain, unstable slopes and erosion. Natural heritage, which would be that wetland and woodlot areas. Also hydrogeology. That's where we would look at any impacts on groundwater, especially potable water. And we also comment on stormwater management and source protection. So we are not the approval authority for planning. Municipalities issue approvals, but we do provide you with comments in all of those technical areas that you take into consideration when making your decisions. So once somebody has nailed down any planning approvals they need, then that's when they would move on to the permit stage. So typically development would need potentially building permits from the municipality and also potentially septic permits. And that may be issued also by the conservation authority of the health unit, depending where you are. And the person may also need approval from the conservation authority for a section 28 permit. And that may be because the development is in an area that's flood plain or interferes with a wetland or involves any sort of watercourse or shoreline alteration. So this slide kind of shows you that municipalities are responsible for approving planning applications, building permits and septic permits, and conservation authorities only comment at the planning stage. And then we have a role of issuing permits at the permit stage. But it shows you very much who's responsible for what and how the municipal role and the CA role work together. The vast majority of permit applications that we receive are approved and the vast majority of planning applications that we review have no objections. So it's important to us that we're offering a service that's efficient and effective, not only for the applicants, but also efficient for the municipalities and the CA. So a few things that we've done in recent years include cutting our review timelines in half. So a couple of years ago, we cut both our timelines for providing municipalities with planning comments, but also our timelines for issuing Section 28 permits in half, and we report those results annually on our website.
